name: G.257

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Licensed in 2023 alongside G.66 and G.484; US plant patent PP35,016.

soil_notes: average to good soils; vigorous enough for replant ground
best_for: high-density orchards wanting bigger fruit and heavy crops from an M.7-class tree
avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted; growers needing long field experience before adopting
variety_fit: Cornell recommends it for SnapDragon and Gala, where it lifts fruit size; patent trials also suggest larger Fuji fruit.
notes: A semi-dwarf in the M.7 vigour class, released in 2023 for high-density plantings where growers want larger fruit and high crop loads. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot and woolly apple aphid, replant tolerant, very low suckering, hardier in winter than M.7, and it tends to raise boron levels in the scion. Experience outside trials is still limited.

name: G.935

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Released in the mid-2000s; US plant patent PP17,063.

support: Stake or trellis; some graft-union breaks were recorded in trials
soil_notes: reasonably fertile, well-drained soil; good on replant ground
best_for: M.26-sized trees in cold, fire-blight-prone regions; tall spindle orchards and supported garden trees
avoid_when: woolly-aphid-prone warm regions; unsupported trees on exposed sites
variety_fit: A standard choice for weak growers such as Honeycrisp; Cornell recommends it (with G.202) for very weak varieties.
notes: Sits between M.9 Pajam 2 and M.26 in size with very high yield efficiency, and is one of the most widely planted Geneva stocks. Resistant to fire blight and crown rot, replant tolerant and very cold hardy (among the best survivors of the 2004-05 New York freezes), but susceptible to woolly apple aphid. In the 2010 NC-140 trial it suckered more than M.26 and lost some trees to graft-union breaks, so give it support.

name: G.969

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York

support: Better anchored than the dwarf Geneva stocks; still support in high-density rows
soil_notes: average soils; more forgiving than dwarfs on lighter ground
best_for: semi-dwarf trees that crop early, in cold or fire-blight regions; garden trees needing less support
avoid_when: where a small tree is wanted at close spacing
variety_fit: Cornell rates it excellent for weak scions such as Honeycrisp.
notes: A semi-dwarf between M.26 and M.7 (Cornell's 2024 chart puts it at the M.26 end) that bears far earlier and more efficiently than M.7. Resistant to fire blight, crown rot, powdery mildew and woolly apple aphid, winter hardy, and better anchored than the dwarf Geneva stocks.

name: G.814

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Trialled as CG.4814 (2010 NC-140 trial); US plant patent PP27,643.

support: Trellis or stake; graft-union breaks occurred in trials
soil_notes: fertile, well-drained soil; fine, branched roots and good calcium supply to the fruit
best_for: high-density orchards wanting an M.26-sized, replant-tolerant, fire-blight-resistant stock
avoid_when: scionwood that may carry apple stem grooving virus; woolly-aphid-prone regions; unsupported trees
variety_fit: Use virus-free scions; Honeycrisp fruit on it ran smaller than on M.26 in NC-140.
notes: Roughly M.26-sized (small semi-dwarf after 5 years, large dwarf after 8 in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial) with good precocity and yield efficiency, fire blight and crown rot resistance, replant tolerance and good calcium uptake. Weak points are woolly apple aphid susceptibility, sensitivity to apple stem grooving virus, and the second-highest mortality in that trial (24% after 8 years, from graft-union breaks and some fire blight losses in Mexico).

name: CG.4013

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Unreleased selection; evaluated in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp and Fuji trials.

support: Trellised in trials; support in high-density systems
avoid_when: commercial or garden planting - not released
variety_fit: Only Honeycrisp and Fuji data published (NC-140).
notes: An unreleased Cornell-Geneva selection known mainly from the 2010 NC-140 trials. With Honeycrisp it began as a large dwarf but was a small semi-dwarf after 8 years (trunk area about 20% above M.26), suckered about as heavily as M.9 Pajam 2, and its cumulative yield efficiency was only around M.26 level. Survival was 95%, including 100% at the Minnesota and Wisconsin sites; one tree was lost to fire blight in Mexico.

name: CG.5087

origin.place: Cornell University / USDA-ARS apple rootstock breeding program, Geneva, New York
origin.note: Unreleased selection; evaluated in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial.

support: Trellised in trials; support in high-density systems
avoid_when: commercial or garden planting - not released
variety_fit: Only Honeycrisp data published; fruit ran smaller than on M.26.
notes: An unreleased Cornell-Geneva selection; in the 2010 NC-140 Honeycrisp trial it grouped with M.26 and M.9 Pajam 2 as a large dwarf after 8 years and was among the most yield-efficient in that class, with higher projected per-hectare yield than M.26. Survival was 91% (100% at the Minnesota and Wisconsin sites) and suckering was similar to M.26, though Honeycrisp fruit averaged smaller. No published disease-resistance ratings were found.

name: V.1

origin.parentage: open-pollinated seedling from 'Kerr' crabapple and M.9 material
origin.note: Vineland series selected by A. Hutchinson; tested in the 1994 NC-140 dwarf trial; nursery supply from about 2003.

soil_notes: few soil-specific data; treat like M.26 (fertile, well-drained)
best_for: M.26-sized trees in cold-winter regions of Canada and the northern US where fire blight is a risk
avoid_when: unsupported trees; regions where it cannot be sourced
variety_fit: No notable scion problems reported in NC-140 trials.
notes: An M.26-class dwarf from Ontario; after 10 years in the 1994 NC-140 trial trees were about the size of M.26 EMLA with similar or better yield efficiency, excellent survival, and few suckers or burr knots. Reported as cold hardy and, unlike M.26, fairly to highly resistant to fire blight. Mostly of interest in Canada and the northern US.

name: Antonovka 313

origin.parentage: Antonovka-derived selection; exact origin poorly documented
origin.note: Evaluated at about 18 North American sites in the 1984 NC-140 trial.

support: Free-standing; trees may lean on exposed sites
soil_notes: adapted to a wide range of soils
best_for: full-size free-standing trees in northern regions
avoid_when: small gardens; sites prone to late-winter freeze-thaw swings
variety_fit: Too vigorous for most modern spacing except with spur-type or weak varieties.
notes: A standard-size, free-standing stock of Russian origin that is slow to crop but was slightly more productive and efficient than seedling in the 1984 NC-140 trial, with good survival across many sites. Despite nursery claims of extreme hardiness, US sources rate it only moderately hardy and prone to late-winter injury. Reported resistant to crown rot (though it rotted under heavy artificial inoculation in California), moderately susceptible to fire blight, with some suckers and few burr knots.
